```

```{r cran-gate, include = FALSE}
# The model fits below are evaluated when the article is built locally, in CI

# there the code is shown without being run.
EVAL_FITS <- identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true")
# The data and the polygon operations come from sf; the neighbour cross-check
# uses spdep. Both are suggested packages, so the article runs only with them.
has_sf    <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = EVAL_FITS && has_sf)
```

This article analyses a real dataset from start to finish: counts of sudden
infant death syndrome (SIDS) in the 100 counties of North Carolina. The
question is whether counties with a larger share of non-white births have a
higher SIDS risk once neighbouring counties are allowed to share unmeasured
risk. It ends with a map of each county's relative risk, the probability that
the risk exceeds the state average, and a list of what the data can and cannot
answer. The data ship with [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/), which also
reads the county polygons; [spdep](https://r-spatial.github.io/spdep/) is used
once to cross-check the neighbour graph. The model family itself is introduced
in [Spatial models](spatial-models.html), which fits the same fields to
simulated data with a known truth.

Installation is covered in [Get started](tulpa.html).

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
library(sf)
```

## The data

The file `nc.shp` in sf holds one polygon per county and, for two periods
(1974-78 and 1979-84), the number of live births (`BIR74`, `BIR79`), the
number of SIDS deaths (`SID74`, `SID79`) and the number of non-white live
births (`NWBIR74`, `NWBIR79`). sf documents it as the North Carolina SIDS
sample data (`?sf::nc`); the counts were analysed for spatial clustering by
Cressie and Read (1985) and Cressie and Chan (1989). The polygons are stored
in longitude and latitude (NAD27). Transform them to the North Carolina state
plane (EPSG 32119), a planar system in metres, so that boundaries and
centroids are computed on a flat map.

```{r read}
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
nc <- st_transform(nc, 32119)
dim(nc)
```

Most of the analysis uses the first period. The deaths are rare: a county
with few births may record none, and the raw rate of such a county says
little.

```{r counts}
summary(nc$SID74)
sum(nc$SID74 == 0)
```

Risk is compared through the expected count $E_i$: the number of deaths
county $i$ would have if every county shared the statewide rate,
$E_i = B_i \sum_j D_j / \sum_j B_j$, with $B_i$ the births and $D_i$ the
deaths of county $i$. The ratio $D_i / E_i$ is the standardised mortality
ratio (SMR). The covariate is the share of non-white births, centred at its
mean across counties and multiplied by 10, so that its coefficient is the
change in log relative risk per 10 percentage points.

```{r prepare}
nc$E   <- nc$BIR74 * sum(nc$SID74) / sum(nc$BIR74)
nc$smr <- nc$SID74 / nc$E
nc$pnw <- nc$NWBIR74 / nc$BIR74
pnw_mean <- mean(nc$pnw)
nc$x <- 10 * (nc$pnw - pnw_mean)
round(pnw_mean, 3)
round(range(nc$smr), 2)
```

```{r map-smr, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Map of North Carolina counties coloured by the standardised mortality ratio for SIDS in 1974-78, from below 0.5 to above 2"}
br <- c(0, 0.5, 0.8, 1, 1.25, 2, 5)
plot(nc["smr"], breaks = br, pal = hcl.colors(6, "Blue-Red 3"),
     main = "SMR, 1974-78", key.pos = 1)
```

```{r map-pnw, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Map of North Carolina counties coloured by the share of non-white births in 1974-78, highest in the north-east and the south"}
plot(nc["pnw"], pal = function(k) hcl.colors(k, "Greens 3", rev = TRUE),
     main = "Share of non-white births", key.pos = 1)
```

The mean non-white share across counties is 31.2%. The SMR runs from zero, in
the 13 counties without a recorded death, to 4.73, and neighbouring counties
often fall in classes far apart. High SMRs gather in the north-east and the
south of the state, the same two regions where the non-white share is
highest.

## The model

Write $y_i$ for the SIDS deaths of county $i = 1, \ldots, 100$ and $x_i$ for
its scaled non-white share. The counts are modelled as Poisson around the
expected count times a relative risk $\theta_i$:

$$
y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(E_i\,\theta_i), \qquad
\log \theta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \phi_i .
$$

Taking logs, $\log E_i$ enters the linear predictor with coefficient one;
this fixed term is the offset. $\beta_0$ is the log relative risk of a county
at the mean non-white share, $\beta_1$ the change per 10 percentage points,
and $\phi_i$ a county effect that carries the part of the risk the covariate
does not explain. The non-spatial model sets $\phi_i = 0$.

Two priors for $\phi$ tie each county to its neighbours. The intrinsic
conditional autoregression (ICAR) centres each $\phi_i$ on the mean of its
neighbours, with a precision $\tau$ that sets how strongly they agree. BYM2
writes the field as a mix of a scaled ICAR part and an independent part per
county, with an overall standard deviation $\sigma$ and a share $\rho$ of the
variance that is spatially structured. Both are written out in
[Spatial models](spatial-models.html); here they are compared on the same
counties.

## Building the neighbour graph

Two counties are neighbours when their polygons share a boundary point.
`adjacency()` builds that graph directly from the polygons; `id = "FIPS"`
records the county code of each node, so the graph can be matched to the data
by key.

```{r adjacency}
g <- adjacency(nc, id = "FIPS")
g
```

`check_adjacency()` confirms that the matrix is symmetric and binary, and,
for an intrinsic field, the property that matters most: the graph has one
connected component and no county without neighbours.

```{r check}
chk <- check_adjacency(g$adjacency)
```

The same contiguity rule in spdep gives the same matrix:

```{r spdep-check, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_sf && has_spdep}
nb <- spdep::poly2nb(nc, queen = TRUE)
W_spdep <- spdep::nb2mat(nb, style = "B")
all(W_spdep == as.matrix(g$adjacency))
```

The model needs a column mapping each row of the data to a node of the graph.
`node_index()` looks the county code up in the graph. Build the data frame the
fits use, with one row per county:

```{r data-frame}
W <- as.matrix(g$adjacency)
d <- st_drop_geometry(nc)[, c("NAME", "FIPS", "SID74", "E", "x")]
d$county <- node_index(g, d$FIPS)
head(d, 3)
```

## A non-spatial fit

The offset enters the formula as `offset(log(E))`. Fit the Poisson model
without a county effect first:

```{r fit-nonspatial}
fit0 <- tulpa(SID74 ~ x + offset(log(E)), data = d,
              family = "poisson", mode = "laplace")
summary(fit0)
```

The slope is 0.187 per 10 percentage points, with a standard error of 0.022.
Exponentiated, its interval bounds give the ratio of the relative risks of two
counties whose non-white shares differ by 10 percentage points:

```{r rr-nonspatial}
round(exp(confint(fit0)["x", ]), 3)
```

## Residual spatial structure

A spatial term is justified when the residuals of the non-spatial fit still
cluster on the map. `moran_i()` tests that with Moran's I on a set of
neighbour weights. With polygons, the coordinates are the county centroids,
and the five nearest neighbours of each centroid stand in for the contiguity
graph, whose mean is 4.9 neighbours per county.

Start with the raw risk: the Pearson residuals of a model with an intercept
only.

```{r moran-raw}
cc <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(nc)))
fit_int <- tulpa(SID74 ~ 1 + offset(log(E)), data = d,
                 family = "poisson", mode = "laplace")
moran_i(fit_int, cc, weights = "knn", k = 5)
```

Then the residuals after the covariate:

```{r moran-nonspatial}
moran_i(fit0, cc, weights = "knn", k = 5)
```

The raw risk clusters: Moran's I is 0.274, against an expectation of -0.010
under no autocorrelation (p < 0.001). After the covariate, I falls to 0.038
(p = 0.41), so most of the clustering of the raw rates follows the map of the
non-white share, which is clustered itself. A test on 100 counties may still
miss weak residual structure, and a field changes the uncertainty of the
slope even where the test finds none, which the next section shows.

## Spatial fits

An areal field takes two pieces: `spatial = list(type =, adjacency =)` carries
the graph, and a `spatial(county)` term in the formula names the column that
maps rows to nodes. `mode = "nested_laplace"` integrates the field's
hyperparameters over a grid.

```{r fit-icar}
fit_icar <- tulpa(SID74 ~ x + offset(log(E)) + spatial(county), data = d,
                  family = "poisson",
                  spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
                  mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
summary(fit_icar)
```

The slope moves from 0.187 to 0.197 and its standard error from 0.022 to
0.034. The field's precision $\tau$ has a posterior mean of 9.2 and a 95%
interval from 2.6 to 39. As a standard deviation, $1/\sqrt{\tau}$, that is
between 0.16 and 0.62 on the log relative-risk scale. The reliability line
calls the outer integration borderline: the grid weight sits on 3.8 effective
cells out of 9, so the interval for $\tau$ is resolved to about one grid cell.
`diagnostics(fit_icar)` gives the full report.

BYM2 adds an independent part per county to the ICAR field:

```{r fit-bym2}
fit_bym2 <- tulpa(SID74 ~ x + offset(log(E)) + spatial(county), data = d,
                  family = "poisson",
                  spatial = list(type = "bym2", adjacency = W),
                  mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
summary(fit_bym2)
```

BYM2 gives the same slope, 0.197 with a standard error of 0.033. Its field
has a standard deviation of 0.27 (95% interval 0.12 to 0.42) on the log
relative-risk scale. The structured share $\rho$ has an interval from 0.09 to
0.97, so 100 counties leave open how much of the county variation is shared
with neighbours and how much is independent. The summary reports no
reliability verdict for this grid ("not computed").

The three slopes side by side, as relative risks per 10 percentage points:

```{r slopes}
fits <- list(nonspatial = fit0, icar = fit_icar, bym2 = fit_bym2)
slope_row <- function(f) unlist(coef(summary(f))["x", ])
slopes <- t(sapply(fits, slope_row))
round(exp(slopes[, c(1, 3, 4)]), 3)
round(slopes[, "std.error"], 3)
```

All three fits put the relative risk per 10 percentage points at 1.21 or
1.22. The spatial fits widen the interval, with standard errors of 0.033 and
0.034 against 0.022: the field adds county-level variation beyond the Poisson
noise, and the slope's uncertainty grows with it.

## Mapping relative risk

A nested-Laplace fit stores, for every cell of its hyperparameter grid, the
mean and variance of each observation's linear predictor (`fitted_eta` and
`fitted_eta_var`, see `?tulpa_nested_laplace`), offset included. The
posterior of the linear predictor is the mixture of these Gaussians, weighted
by the grid weights `tulpa_outer_grid()` returns. The helper below draws from
that mixture county by county and divides by the expected count, which gives
draws of $\theta_i$.

```{r rr-draws-fn}
rr_draws <- function(fit, E, n = 4000) {
  w   <- tulpa_outer_grid(fit)$weights
  k   <- sample(seq_along(w), n, replace = TRUE, prob = w)
  m   <- fit$fitted_eta[k, , drop = FALSE]
  s   <- sqrt(fit$fitted_eta_var[k, , drop = FALSE])
  eta <- m + s * matrix(rnorm(length(m)), nrow(m))
  sweep(exp(eta), 2, E, "/")
}
```

Each column is one county. Because a draw picks one grid cell for every
county at once but draws the counties independently within it, the columns
give each county's own posterior correctly; a quantity that combines several
counties (a ranking, a regional total) would need their joint covariance,
which the fit does not keep.

```{r rr-summary}
set.seed(1)
th <- rr_draws(fit_bym2, d$E)
nc$rr      <- colMeans(th)
nc$rr_sd   <- apply(th, 2, sd)
nc$p_exc   <- colMeans(th > 1)
summary(nc$rr)
round(range(nc$rr[nc$SID74 == 0]), 2)
```

```{r map-rr, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Map of North Carolina counties coloured by the BYM2 posterior mean relative risk, on the same colour classes as the SMR map"}
plot(nc["rr"], breaks = br, pal = hcl.colors(6, "Blue-Red 3"),
     main = "Relative risk, BYM2 posterior mean", key.pos = 1)
```

On the same colour classes, the fitted risks span a narrower range than the
SMRs, from 0.52 to 2.51 against 0 to 4.73. The 13 counties without a recorded
death get fitted risks from 0.52 to 1.48, set by their non-white share and
their neighbours.

```{r map-sd, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Map of North Carolina counties coloured by the posterior standard deviation of the relative risk"}
plot(nc["rr_sd"], pal = function(k) hcl.colors(k, "Purples 3", rev = TRUE),
     main = "Posterior SD of the relative risk", key.pos = 1)
```

The posterior standard deviation shows how well each county's risk is
determined:

```{r sd-facts}
summary(nc$rr_sd)
nc$NAME[which.max(nc$rr_sd)]
round(cor(nc$rr, nc$rr_sd), 2)
```

The standard deviation runs from 0.12 to 0.67, largest in Anson County, and
its correlation with the posterior mean across counties is 0.89. The risk is
the exponential of a roughly Gaussian linear predictor, so its standard
deviation grows with its mean, and the map above largely repeats the risk
map. The probability that the risk exceeds one combines the two into a single
number per county:

```{r map-exc, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Map of North Carolina counties coloured by the posterior probability that the relative risk exceeds one, in classes below 0.05, 0.05 to 0.2, 0.2 to 0.8, 0.8 to 0.95 and above 0.95"}
plot(nc["p_exc"], breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.2, 0.8, 0.95, 1),
     pal = hcl.colors(5, "Blue-Red 3"),
     main = "P(relative risk > 1)", key.pos = 1)
```

The exceedance probability reads off which counties the data place above the
state average with some confidence:

```{r exceed}
sum(nc$p_exc > 0.95)
sum(nc$p_exc < 0.05)
head(st_drop_geometry(nc)[order(-nc$p_exc),
                          c("NAME", "SID74", "smr", "rr", "p_exc")], 5)
```

In 18 counties the posterior probability that the risk exceeds the state
average is above 0.95, and in 26 it is below 0.05. Anson County has the
largest SMR, 4.73 on 15 deaths, and a fitted risk of 2.51. The counties with
a high exceedance probability lie in the north-east and the south, the
regions with the highest non-white share.

## Residual Moran's I after the spatial fit

`moran_i()` on a tulpa fit reads its residuals at the posterior-mean linear
predictor with the field included (`effects = "conditional"`, the default), so
it tests what the spatial model leaves behind:

```{r moran-after}
moran_i(fit_bym2, cc, weights = "knn", k = 5)
```

Moran's I of these residuals is -0.030 (p = 0.74). The check is weak by
construction: every county has its own field value, so the fitted mean
follows each county's count and the residuals shrink towards zero. A value
near zero says the spatial model leaves no clustering in its residuals; it
does not show that the field has the right form.

## Comparing the models

`compare_models()` ranks the fits by WAIC or PSIS-LOO, both computed from each
fit's pointwise log-likelihood with the field included.

```{r compare-waic}
compare_models(nonspatial = fit0, icar = fit_icar, bym2 = fit_bym2,
               criterion = "waic")
```

```{r compare-loo}
compare_models(nonspatial = fit0, icar = fit_icar, bym2 = fit_bym2,
               criterion = "loo")
```

Both spatial models score higher than the non-spatial one, by an amount
close to its own uncertainty. BYM2 leads the non-spatial fit by 5.5 in
expected log predictive density under WAIC and by 4.6 under LOO, with a
standard error of the difference of 4.0 and 3.9. ICAR and BYM2 differ by
1.1 and 0.6, within one standard error. The effective number of parameters
(`p_eff`) is about 3 for the non-spatial fit and 21 to 24 for the spatial
ones, the cost of one field value per county.

## Sensitivity to the prior on the field

On the nested-Laplace path the field's scale axis carries a penalised
complexity (PC) prior with $P(\sigma > 3) = 0.01$ by default
(`hyperprior = "proper"`, see `?tulpa_nested_laplace`), carried to whichever
of $\sigma$ or $\tau$ the axis integrates. `hyperprior = "flat"` removes it,
so the field's scale is integrated under the grid's own measure. Refit both
spatial models that way:

```{r fit-flat}
fit_icar_flat <- tulpa(
  SID74 ~ x + offset(log(E)) + spatial(county), data = d,
  family = "poisson", spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
  mode = "nested_laplace", hyperprior = "flat",
  control = list(n_threads = 2))
fit_bym2_flat <- tulpa(
  SID74 ~ x + offset(log(E)) + spatial(county), data = d,
  family = "poisson", spatial = list(type = "bym2", adjacency = W),
  mode = "nested_laplace", hyperprior = "flat",
  control = list(n_threads = 2))
```

The slope and the field hyperparameters under the two priors:

```{r prior-table}
pfits <- list(icar_pc = fit_icar, icar_flat = fit_icar_flat,
              bym2_pc = fit_bym2, bym2_flat = fit_bym2_flat)
round(t(sapply(pfits, slope_row)), 3)
hyp <- lapply(pfits, function(f)
  summary(f)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")])
do.call(rbind, hyp)
```

Under every prior the slope is 0.196 or 0.197, with standard errors within
0.002 of each other. The posterior of the field's scale changes
in its tail: the ICAR precision's interval runs from 2.7 to 54 under the flat
prior against 2.6 to 39 under the PC prior, and the BYM2 standard deviation
from 0.09 to 0.40 against 0.12 to 0.42. For an areal field `tulpa()` offers
these two choices; the PC prior's anchor is fixed at $P(\sigma > 3) = 0.01$
on this path ([Priors](priors.html)).

## A second period

The 1979-84 counts give a second look at the same counties. Rebuild the
expected counts and the covariate from the later columns, keeping the
1974-78 mean for the centring so that $x = 0$ means the same share in both
periods, and refit the BYM2 model:

```{r fit-79}
d79 <- st_drop_geometry(nc)[, c("FIPS", "SID79", "BIR79", "NWBIR79")]
d79$E <- d79$BIR79 * sum(d79$SID79) / sum(d79$BIR79)
d79$x <- 10 * (d79$NWBIR79 / d79$BIR79 - pnw_mean)
d79$county <- node_index(g, d79$FIPS)
fit_bym2_79 <- tulpa(SID79 ~ x + offset(log(E)) + spatial(county),
                     data = d79, family = "poisson",
                     spatial = list(type = "bym2", adjacency = W),
                     mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
round(exp(coef(summary(fit_bym2_79))["x", c(1, 3, 4)]), 3)
```

The later period gives a weaker association: a relative risk of 1.07 per 10
percentage points, with an interval from 1.003 to 1.144. That interval ends
where the 1974-78 interval (1.142 to 1.302) begins, so the two periods agree
that the association is positive and differ on its size.

## What the data can and cannot say

Across the counties of North Carolina in 1974-78, a higher share of non-white
births goes with a higher SIDS rate: a relative risk of about 1.21 per 10
percentage points in every model fitted here. Allowing neighbouring counties
to share unmeasured risk leaves that estimate where it was and widens its
interval by about half. The clustering of the raw rates largely follows the
covariate, which is itself clustered on the map.

The estimate compares counties, and it cannot be carried over to infants. The
data record deaths per county, without the race of the infants who died, so a
county-level slope of this size is consistent with many individual-level
patterns, including ones in which the excess deaths in high-share counties
occur among white infants. Reading a group-level association as an
individual-level one is the ecological fallacy. The non-white share may also
stand for other county characteristics the data do not contain, such as
income or access to care, so the slope describes an association between
county rates and is not a causal effect of the share.

One hundred counties set the precision of everything above. The BYM2 split
between structured and independent county effects is left almost entirely
open ($\rho$ between 0.09 and 0.97), the predictive gain of the spatial models
is 4.6 to 5.5 against a standard error of about 4.0, and the second period puts the
association at 1.07 instead of 1.22. A single county's risk rests on its own
few deaths plus what its neighbours and covariate lend it; the exceedance map
separates 18 counties above the state average and 26 below it with
probability 0.95, and leaves the remaining 56 undecided.
